entries.name: The locked-room mystery
entries.description: A crime committed inside a space that appears sealed from the inside, with no apparent way in or out for a culprit.

examples.work: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes ("The Speckled Band")
examples.text: Doyle sets up a bedroom sealed by a stuck bell-rope, a ventilator that shouldn't exist, and a bed bolted to the floor — every detail apparently decorative until Holmes reveals the room was built as a murder device, its "locked" nature explained by a trained snake entering through the false ventilator. The trope's core pleasure, the reader re-reading the crime scene and realizing every strange detail was a clue, is executed almost perfectly here.

examples.work: The Hollow Man (also published as The Three Coffins)
examples.text: Carr devotes an entire chapter to Dr. Gideon Fell lecturing directly to the reader on the taxonomy of locked-room solutions — a genuinely useful primer for any writer attempting the form — before delivering a case with two impossible crimes and a snow-covered street with no footprints. It remains the genre's most self-aware and most cited locked-room novel.

entries.name: The drawing-room denouement
entries.description: The detective gathers every suspect in one room and walks the group through the solution live, unmasking the culprit in front of the other suspects.

examples.text: Poirot's gathered-room reveal is the genre's most structurally audacious use of the device, because the detective is explicitly addressing the narrator as much as the suspects, and the narrator has been the culprit the entire time. The scene works because Christie plays scrupulously fair with the physical clues even while the narrator's account has quietly omitted the truth.

Johnson stages a classic drawing-room gathering early in the film, then deliberately breaks the trope by having detective Benoit Blanc admit he doesn't yet know the answer — subverting audience expectation that this scene is always the reveal, and saving the real gathered-suspects unmasking for a redesigned final act that plays the convention straighter.

entries.name: Fingerprint identification
entries.description: Using the unique ridge patterns on a person's fingertips to place them at a scene or match them to a print left on an object.

examples.text: Doyle wrote before fingerprint identification was standard forensic practice in Britain (Scotland Yard didn't adopt it until 1901); Holmes relies instead on footprints, tobacco ash, and physical build. Useful as a reminder that the Holmes canon predates the technology now considered a genre baseline — a writer setting a case in this period should treat fingerprinting as cutting-edge or not-yet-arrived, not assumed.

Though not using fingerprints specifically, Holmes's insistence on examining physical trace evidence at a scene before anyone else contaminates it — footprints in mud, a windowsill's marks — anticipates the crime-scene-integrity principle that modern fingerprint and forensic collection depends on entirely.

entries.name: Poison and toxicology detection
entries.description: Identifying a poison used in a crime through its chemical signature, physiological effects, or residue.

examples.text: Holmes's introduction to the reader includes his own invented test for detecting bloodstains, described as more sensitive than the guaiacum test actually in use at the time — Doyle giving his detective a fictional edge over real 1880s forensic chemistry that makes the character feel ahead of his era rather than merely competent within it.

Not a detective novel, but useful as a negative example: the book treats poison symbolically rather than procedurally, with no interest in detection or diagnosis. Included here as a reminder that "poison in fiction" and "poison as a detective-fiction clue" are different craft problems — the latter requires the poison's effects and detection method to be internally consistent enough for a fair-play reveal.

entries.name: Locard's exchange principle
entries.description: Every contact leaves a trace — the foundational assumption underneath all forensic detective work.
entries.principle: Formulated by French criminologist Edmond Locard in the early 20th century: "every contact leaves a trace." When two objects or people come into contact, material is exchanged between them — fibers, hair, skin cells, soil, residue — and that exchange, however microscopic, is in principle detectable. It is the single organizing assumption underneath fingerprint work, trace fiber analysis, and modern DNA forensics alike.
entries.example: Locard developed the principle while running one of the first forensic laboratories, in Lyon, France, and used it to solve cases via microscopic analysis of dust and fibers found under suspects' fingernails and on their clothing — a discipline barely imagined in Holmes's own era but a direct descendant of Holmes's fictional method of scrutinizing overlooked physical detail.
entries.application: A detective character built on this principle should treat every scene as a two-way exchange: the criminal leaves something behind, and the criminal carries something away. A satisfying fair-play mystery can be built by planting one clue of each kind — something left at the scene, and something the culprit is later found still carrying.

entries.name: Forensic entomology and time of death
entries.description: Using the life cycle of insects found on a body to estimate how long it has been dead.
entries.principle: Blowflies typically arrive at a body within minutes of death and lay eggs; the eggs progress through predictable larval stages at rates that depend on temperature and species. By identifying which insect life stages are present, an examiner can estimate a fairly precise window since death, often tighter than temperature-based estimates alone can provide.
entries.example: The method dates to 13th-century China (a magistrate's manual, the Xi Yuan Ji Lu, describes using fly activity to identify a murder weapon by the blood residue flies were drawn to) and was formalized as modern forensic entomology in the late 19th and 20th centuries — meaning a Holmes-era detective could plausibly know of it as an emerging or half-formed technique, not yet standard practice.
entries.application: Useful for any case where the timeline hinges on exactly when a body was left somewhere versus when it was found — a detective citing insect stages to contradict a suspect's alibi is a period-plausible, scientifically real deduction rather than a hand-wave.

entries.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
entries.description: Creator of Sherlock Holmes; the writer who turned Poe's invention into the genre's most durable franchise.
entries.knownFor: A Scottish physician who began writing Holmes stories to supplement a struggling medical practice, Doyle produced four novels and fifty-six short stories about the detective over four decades, along with historical fiction, science fiction (the Professor Challenger stories), and — notoriously — earnest advocacy for spiritualism late in life. He tried repeatedly to kill Holmes off and retire the character; public demand brought him back each time.
entries.signature: The Holmes stories run on the deduction-as-showmanship set piece (reading a stranger's history from physical detail before they've spoken) and the Watson narrator device. Doyle's prose is brisk, plot-forward, and unafraid of melodrama; the short-story case-of-the-week format, serialized in The Strand Magazine, shaped how popular fiction would be published for the next century.

entries.name: Agatha Christie
entries.description: The best-selling novelist of all time; formalized the fair-play puzzle-box mystery.
entries.knownFor: Created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple across more than sixty novels, and is credited with perfecting the "fair play" contract between author and reader — every clue the detective uses to solve the case is shown to the reader in plain sight before the reveal. Also wrote the West End's longest-running play, The Mousetrap.
entries.signature: Closed-circle settings (a country house, a train, an island) that keep the suspect pool small and knowable; the honest red herring, built from selective emphasis rather than any lie to the reader; and a gathered-room reveal that walks back through the clue trail in front of the assembled suspects.

works.title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
works.note: the novel that broke the genre's rules about narrator trust

works.title: Murder on the Orient Express
works.note: twelve suspects, one confined train car

works.title: And Then There Were None
works.note: ten strangers, an island, no detective at all

entries.name: The Moonstone
entries.description: Often called the first true detective novel; a stolen Indian diamond, multiple unreliable narrators, and Sergeant Cuff.
entries.author: Wilkie Collins
entries.text: Collins tells the theft of a cursed yellow diamond through a relay of narrators — a butler, a religious zealot, a lawyer, the detective himself — each account partial and each narrator carrying their own blind spots, with the truth assembled by the reader from the gaps between them. T.S. Eliot called it "the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels." Sergeant Cuff, the working-class professional detective who solves the case through patient physical observation, is a direct ancestor of both Holmes and every procedural detective who followed. The novel is also notable for its clear-eyed, sympathetic (if period-limited) treatment of opium addiction as a plot mechanism rather than a moral judgment.

entries.name: The Nine Tailors
entries.description: Lord Peter Wimsey investigates a body found in a Fenland churchyard, with English bell-ringing as both setting and murder method.
entries.author: Dorothy L. Sayers
entries.text: Sayers builds the novel around campanology (the art of bell-ringing) with an obsessive, genuinely researched depth that turns technical exposition into atmosphere rather than a lecture — a model for any writer trying to make a specialist subject carry a mystery's plot without boring the reader. The murder method itself, revealed only at the very end, depends entirely on that technical knowledge, making it one of the cleanest examples in the genre of Chekhov's gun executed through subject-matter research rather than a planted object. Wimsey himself is at his most reflective and least flippant here, a mark of Sayers's ambition to let her detective actually carry emotional weight rather than remain a fixed comic type.

entries.name: Golden Age fair-play mystery
entries.description: The puzzle-box tradition where every clue is shown to the reader before the reveal.
entries.principle: Flourished roughly 1920-1950, dominated by British writers (Christie, Sayers, Marsh, Allingham — sometimes called the "Queens of Crime"). The genre's implicit contract: the reader has, in principle, everything needed to solve the case before the detective explains it. Plot puzzle takes precedence over psychological depth or social realism; the closed-circle setting (country house, train, island) keeps the suspect pool manageable.
entries.example: Ronald Knox's 1929 "Ten Commandments of Detective Fiction" codified the era's fair-play rules explicitly — no undisclosed twins, no unknown poisons, no last-minute confessions from characters never previously introduced — a genuinely useful checklist for any writer working in this mode today.
entries.application: Choose this mode when the pleasure you want the reader to have is the game itself — matching wits with the author. Requires rigorous clue-planting discipline: every fact the detective uses in the reveal must have been visible to the reader earlier, even if its significance wasn't.

entries.name: Hardboiled / noir
entries.description: The morally compromised private eye moving through a corrupt city he can't fix, only survive.
entries.principle: Emerged in 1920s-40s America (Hammett, Chandler, and the pulp magazine Black Mask), largely as a reaction against the Golden Age's genteel puzzle-box mode. The detective is often as morally ambiguous as the criminals; the case is frequently an excuse to tour a corrupt social landscape rather than a clean logical puzzle. Prose style — terse, metaphor-driven, voice-forward — carries as much weight as plot.
entries.example: Raymond Chandler's 1944 essay "The Simple Art of Murder" is the genre's own manifesto, explicitly attacking the fair-play puzzle tradition as bloodless and arguing crime fiction should be about "a real world, a world in which gangsters can rule nations."
entries.application: Choose this mode when the book wants moral weight and atmosphere over airtight puzzle logic — a detective changed or worn down by the case, rather than one who solves it and walks away unbothered. Plot looseness is a stylistic choice here, not a flaw, but only works if the reader isn't expecting Christie-style fairness.

entries.name: The founding of Scotland Yard's detective branch
entries.description: The real institutional backdrop against which every Holmes/Lestrade scene plays out.
entries.principle: London's Metropolitan Police was founded in 1829; a dedicated plainclothes Detective Branch followed only in 1842, with just eight officers. It was renamed the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in 1878 after a corruption scandal forced a reorganization. By the time Doyle began writing Holmes in the 1880s, the CID was still a young, professionally insecure institution — which is part of why Lestrade's mix of pride and dependence on Holmes reads as historically plausible rather than merely a genre convention.
entries.example: The Metropolitan Police's failure to catch Jack the Ripper in 1888 — contemporaneous with the Holmes stories' setting — badly damaged public confidence in official detective work and fed exactly the cultural appetite for a private, unofficial genius detective that Doyle was writing into.
entries.application: A writer wanting Scotland Yard characters to feel period-accurate rather than generic should lean into this institutional insecurity — official detectives in this era have real reason to resent a gifted amateur's success, because their own institution's competence is publicly in question.

entries.name: The Bertillon system and the shift to fingerprinting
entries.description: How Victorian-era police identified repeat criminals before fingerprinting was standard.
entries.principle: Alphonse Bertillon, a French police clerk, developed "bertillonage" in the 1880s: a system of precise anatomical measurements (skull width, arm length, ear shape) used to identify individuals and catch repeat offenders under aliases. It was the dominant identification method in police work through the 1890s, before fingerprint classification (developed by Francis Galton, refined by Edward Henry) proved faster and more reliable and displaced it in the early 1900s.
entries.example: Scotland Yard adopted the Henry fingerprint classification system in 1901 — meaning a case set any time before then is historically accurate to have investigators relying on Bertillon-style measurement or simple eyewitness recognition rather than fingerprint matching.
entries.application: For a period-accurate Holmes-era case, a fingerprint left at a scene should be a mysterious, barely-understood clue rather than an instantly actionable one — the technology to exploit it systematically doesn't fully exist yet. This is a useful, historically grounded source of investigative frustration.

entries.name: Eyewitness memory unreliability
entries.description: Human memory is reconstructive, not a recording — eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than it feels to the witness.
entries.principle: Memory does not store events like video; it reconstructs them each time they're recalled, and each reconstruction is vulnerable to distortion from later information, suggestion, stress, and the passage of time. Confidence in a memory does not correlate reliably with its accuracy — a witness can be utterly certain and utterly wrong.
entries.example: Elizabeth Loftus's research from the 1970s onward, including the famous "lost in the mall" studies, demonstrated that false memories can be implanted through suggestive questioning alone — work that has since reshaped how courts treat eyewitness testimony and contributed to numerous wrongful-conviction exonerations.
entries.application: A detective who treats every witness account as provisional — cross-checking it against physical evidence rather than trusting it outright — reads as more realistically skilled than one who takes testimony at face value. Conflicting witness accounts are a legitimate, research-grounded source of red herrings, not just a convenient plot device.

entries.name: Confirmation bias in investigation
entries.description: The tendency to notice and favor evidence that fits a theory already formed, and overlook what contradicts it.
entries.principle: Once an investigator forms a working theory of a case, they tend to interpret ambiguous evidence as supporting that theory and to discount or explain away evidence that doesn't — not through dishonesty, but as a basic feature of how human reasoning works under uncertainty.
entries.example: Confirmation bias is cited as a contributing factor in numerous real wrongful convictions, where investigators fixated on an early suspect and subsequently interpreted ambiguous forensic evidence in that suspect's favor while under-investigating alternative leads.
entries.application: A genuinely brilliant fictional detective should be distinguished from a merely confident one partly by visible resistance to this bias — actively searching for evidence that would disprove their own leading theory, not just evidence that confirms it. This is a strong differentiator between a Holmes-type figure and a lesser, more ordinary investigator in the same story.

entries.name: Clue visibility and the fair-play rule
entries.description: Every fact the detective uses in the final reveal must have been shown to the reader earlier, even if its significance wasn't clear at the time.
entries.principle: The reader should be able to look back after the reveal and find every clue in the text — not necessarily understood, but present. A solution built on information withheld from the reader (an unmentioned twin, an undisclosed poison, a fact revealed only in the final chapter) breaks the genre's central promise and reads as a cheat, however clever it seems to the writer.
entries.example: Ronald Knox's 1929 "Ten Commandments" and the "Detection Club" oath he helped formalize among Golden Age writers (including Christie and Sayers) were explicit attempts to codify this rule after readers began complaining about unfair mysteries — a genre self-regulating its own contract with its audience.
entries.application: When drafting a reveal, work backward: list every fact the detective states in the denouement, then check each one appears on the page earlier. If a fact appears for the first time in the reveal itself, either plant it earlier or cut it from the solution.

entries.name: Constructing an honest red herring
entries.description: A false lead that misdirects the reader without lying to them — built from selective emphasis, not fabricated evidence.
entries.principle: A red herring works by giving a suspect a real motive, a real opportunity, and a plausible-looking piece of evidence — then letting the reader's own assumptions do the misdirecting. The trick is emphasis, not deception: everything shown about the false suspect should be true, just incomplete or interpreted the way the reader naturally would.
entries.example: Christie's method, most visible in Murder on the Orient Express, is to give nearly every character on the page a genuine, independently sufficient motive — so the red herrings aren't fake clues at all, just true ones that happen to point at the wrong (or, famously in that book, an insufficiently singular) conclusion.
entries.application: Give your false suspect the same density of real, checkable detail you give your real culprit. A red herring built on a lie the narrative later has to retract feels like a cheat; a red herring built on true facts arranged to invite the wrong conclusion feels like fair play, even in hindsight.

entries.name: Fair-play audit
entries.description: Confirm every clue the detective uses in the reveal was actually shown to the reader beforehand.
items: List every fact the detective cites in the final reveal, one line each
For each fact, find the earlier page where it was shown to the reader
If a fact appears for the first time in the reveal, either plant it earlier in the draft or cut it from the solution
Check that the culprit had a genuine, demonstrated opportunity to commit the crime as described
Check the detective's method is consistent with how they solved earlier cases in the book

entries.name: Suspect viability checklist
entries.description: Every named suspect should hold up as a plausible culprit until the moment they're cleared.
items: Does this suspect have a real, independently sufficient motive?
Does this suspect have a genuine opportunity, not just proximity?
Is there at least one piece of true evidence that looks bad for them?
Is their eventual innocence explained by something other than the detective simply asserting it?
Could a careful reader have suspected this person seriously, not just in passing?
